formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY24/25 Q1(1)]
Consider a physical link having 8 nine's reliability, what is the probability that this link gets broken?
formulaApplication.explanation:
8 nines means availability r = 0.99999999 (eight 9s).
Break probability b = 1 − r = 0.00000001 = 10⁻⁸.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY24/25 Q1(2)]
Given the network shown in Figure Q1.2 and assume that each link fails independently with a probability of 0.05. What is the probability that SG is disconnected from SF?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Break the graph into 3 independent paths:
1) SG–HW–SF (series): r = 0.95 × 0.95 = 0.9025, so b = 1 − 0.9025 = 0.0975
2) SG–SF upper link: b = 0.05
3) SG–SF lower link: b = 0.05
SG is cut off only if ALL paths break: 0.0975 × 0.05 × 0.05 = 2.44 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 2.4 × 10⁻⁴.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY23/24 Q1(3)]
The probability of a link break between Singapore and Hong Kong is 0.3. Determine the number of parallel links required to ensure that the probability of the link between Singapore and Hong Kong remains connected is above 0.99.
formulaApplication.explanation:
Parallel links: disconnected only if ALL n links break, so P(connected) = 1 − 0.3ⁿ.
n = 3: 1 − 0.027 = 0.973 (not enough)
n = 4: 1 − 0.0081 = 0.9919 > 0.99 ✓
So 4 links.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY25/26 Q1(3)]
Singapore is connected to Japan via Guam, i.e., two independent links SG-Guam and Guam-Tokyo. A Telco company has proposed a direct SG-Tokyo link, on a separate cable system, to improve the availability of the communication between Singapore and Tokyo. The probability that any single communication link failure is 0.1. Determine the availability of the Singapore and Tokyo, i.e., the probability they are connected.
formulaApplication.explanation:
Path 1 (SG–Guam–Tokyo, series): r = 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81, so b = 0.19
Path 2 (direct SG–Tokyo): b = 0.1
Both paths broken: 0.19 × 0.1 = 0.019
Availability = 1 − 0.019 = 0.981.
Trap: 0.81 is just the Guam path on its own.

formulaApplication.question: A carrier-grade link has 6 nines (99.9999%) reliability. Using the definition of failure probability, about how much downtime is allowed per year (365 days)?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Failure probability = fraction of time the link is down.
b = 1 − 0.999999 = 10⁻⁶
Downtime = 10⁻⁶ × (365 × 24 × 3600 s) = 10⁻⁶ × 31,536,000 = 31.5 s.
(5.3 minutes would be 5 nines.)

formulaApplication.question: In the network below, each link breaks independently with probability 0.02. What is the probability that A cannot communicate with D?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Links in series: A reaches D only if all 3 links work.
r = 0.98³ = 0.9412
b = 1 − 0.9412 = 0.0588.
Trap: 0.06 just adds the three break probabilities, and 8 × 10⁻⁶ multiplies them (that's the parallel rule).

formulaApplication.question: Using the break probabilities labelled on each link in the figure (links fail independently), what is the probability that SG is isolated from AU?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Path 1 SG–HW–AU (series): r = 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81, b = 0.19
Path 2 direct SG–AU: b = 0.2
Isolated only if both paths break: 0.19 × 0.2 = 0.038.
0.962 is the availability (connected), not the isolation probability.

formulaApplication.question: SG connects to HW with two independent links, HW connects to SF with one link, and there is also a direct long-range SG–SF link. Every link fails independently with probability 0.1. What is the probability that SG is disconnected from SF?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Step 1, the two parallel SG–HW links act as one: b = 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01, r = 0.99
Step 2, path SG–HW–SF (series): r = 0.99 × 0.9 = 0.891, b = 0.109
Step 3, combine with the direct SG–SF link (b = 0.1): 0.109 × 0.1 = 0.0109 = 1.09 × 10⁻².
This is the same structure as Tutorial 1 Q4, just with 0.1 instead of 0.05.

formulaApplication.question: A connects to D through two independent 2-hop paths: A–B–D and A–C–D. Each of the 4 links breaks independently with probability 0.1. What is the availability between A and D (probability they stay connected)?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Each path is 2 links in series: r = 0.9² = 0.81, b = 0.19
Two paths in parallel: both break with probability 0.19² = 0.0361
Availability = 1 − 0.0361 = 0.9639.
0.9801 wrongly treats each path as if it had only 1 link; 0.0361 is the disconnection probability.

formulaApplication.question: Each submarine cable between two cities breaks independently with probability 0.2. What is the minimum number of parallel cables needed so that the availability is at least 0.9999?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Need P(all n cables break) = 0.2ⁿ ≤ 10⁻⁴.
n = 5: 0.2⁵ = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ (too big)
n = 6: 0.2⁶ = 6.4 × 10⁻⁵ ≤ 10⁻⁴ ✓
So 6 cables.

theory.question: In the OSI 7-layer model, which layer is responsible for path determination and logical addressing?
theory.explanation:
Network layer (layer 3, data unit = packet): path determination + logical addressing.
Data link (layer 2, frame) does physical addressing; transport (layer 4, segment) does end-to-end reliability.

theory.question: At a Service Access Point (SAP), layer n+1 passes data down to layer n. What is this data called, and what does layer n do with it?
options: A) It is an n-PDU, and layer n sends it to its peer without changes
B) It is an n-SAP, and layer n forwards it unchanged
C) It is an n-PDU, and layer n strips the header to form an n-SDU
D) It is an n-SDU, and layer n adds its header to form an n-PDU
E) It is an (n+1)-SDU, and layer n sends it straight to the physical layer
theory.explanation:
Data handed down to layer n is the n-SDU (Service Data Unit).
Layer n encapsulates it by adding its own header H, producing the n-PDU (Protocol Data Unit).
Peer layers talk to each other using PDUs.

theory.question: Which protocol-to-layer pairing in the 5-layer TCP/IP model is INCORRECT?
theory.explanation:
From the lecture:
Application: FTP, SMTP, HTTP
Transport: TCP, UDP
Network: IP, routing protocols
Link: PPP, Ethernet
So Ethernet belongs to the Link layer, not the Network layer.

theory.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the benefits of a layered network architecture listed in the lecture?
options: A) Flexibility: networks can be modified layer by layer
B) Incremental changes: new layers or new functions can be added easily
C) Simplicity: easy to design once layers and their interactions are defined
D) It guarantees the fastest possible implementation
E) A change of one layer's service is transparent to the rest of the system
theory.explanation:
Benefits: simplicity, flexibility, incremental changes (and modular, transparent changes).
The slides even ask 'Layering harmful?' because a clean layered design is not always the most efficient implementation.

theory.question: Which statement about computing network availability is correct?
options: A) For links in parallel, find the probability that all links are broken
B) For a mix of series and parallel links, add up the break probabilities of every link
C) For links in series, find the probability that all links are broken
D) Link availability r and break probability b are related by r = b − 1
E) The method assumes link breaks are dependent on each other
theory.explanation:
Rules from the lecture:
• Series: probability that ALL links work (multiply the r's).
• Parallel: probability that ALL links break (multiply the b's).
• Mixed: decompose into paths (path-based approach).
Assumes independent link breaks, and r = 1 − b.

formulaApplication.question: 5 links are connected in series, each with reliability r = 0.99. What is the reliability of the whole path?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Series: multiply the individual reliabilities.
r_total = 0.99⁵ ≈ 0.951.

formulaApplication.question: 4 identical backup links run in parallel between two routers. Each has a break probability of 0.2. What is the probability that ALL 4 fail at once (the routers become disconnected)?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Parallel: multiply the break probabilities (disconnected only if every link is down).
b_total = 0.2⁴ = 0.0016.

formulaApplication.question: Nodes X, Y and Z form a chain X-Y-Z (2 links in series, r = 0.95 each). There is also a direct long-range X-Z link (r = 0.85), independent of the chain. What is the probability that X is connected to Z?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Chain X-Y-Z (series): r = 0.95×0.95 = 0.9025, so b_chain = 0.0975.
Direct link: b_direct = 0.15.
X is cut off from Z only if BOTH the chain and the direct link fail (parallel rule): b_total = 0.0975×0.15 ≈ 0.0146.
r_total = 1 − 0.0146 ≈ 0.985.

formulaApplication.question: Node A connects to node D via two independent 2-hop paths: A-B-D (each link r = 0.9) and A-C-D (each link r = 0.85). What is the probability A is connected to D?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Path 1 (A-B-D, series): r = 0.9×0.9 = 0.81, b = 0.19
Path 2 (A-C-D, series): r = 0.85×0.85 = 0.7225, b = 0.2775
Connected unless BOTH paths fail (parallel): b_total = 0.19×0.2775 ≈ 0.0527
r_total = 1 − 0.0527 ≈ 0.947.

formulaApplication.question: In the network shown, A and D are linked by A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, and a fifth "bridge" link B-C. Every link has reliability r = 0.9, and all links fail independently. What is the probability A is connected to D?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Condition on the bridge link B-C:
If the bridge is UP (prob 0.9): B and C merge into one node. A reaches it via A-B OR A-C (parallel: r = 1−0.1×0.1 = 0.99), and it reaches D via B-D OR C-D (also 0.99). r(connected | bridge up) = 0.99×0.99 = 0.9801.
If the bridge is DOWN (prob 0.1): it's just the simple two-path case A-B-D parallel with A-C-D, each a series pair (r = 0.81): r(connected | bridge down) = 1−(1−0.81)² = 0.9639.
Total: 0.9×0.9801 + 0.1×0.9639 ≈ 0.978.
This "condition on one link" trick is the standard way to handle a bridge/cross-link that a simple series-parallel decomposition can't handle directly.

formulaApplication.question: A carrier-grade link needs 5 nines (99.999%) reliability. About how much downtime is allowed per WEEK (7 days)?
Each of several identical parallel links has a break probability of 0.15. What is the minimum number of parallel links needed so that overall reliability exceeds 99.9%?

3 independent parallel links connect A to B (r = 0.8 each). That combined link is then in series with 2 independent parallel links connecting B to C (r = 0.85 each). What is the reliability between A and C?
formulaApplication.explanation:
A-B: 3 parallel links, b = 0.2³ = 0.008, so r_AB = 0.992.
B-C: 2 parallel links, b = 0.15² = 0.0225, so r_BC = 0.9775.
A to C is these two combined links in series: r_AC = 0.992 × 0.9775 ≈ 0.970.

formulaApplication.question: Two links are in series: the first has reliability 0.95, the second 0.9. What is the reliability of the path?
formulaApplication.explanation: Series: r_total = 0.95 × 0.9 = 0.855.

formulaApplication.question: 3 unreliable parallel links (r = 0.3 each) are then combined in series with one very reliable link (r = 0.99). What is the overall reliability?
formulaApplication.explanation:
3 parallel links, r = 0.3 each: b = 0.7³ = 0.343, so r_parallel = 0.657.
In series with the r = 0.99 link: r_total = 0.657 × 0.99 ≈ 0.650.

formulaApplication.question: A path is made of 4 identical links in series. What minimum reliability must EACH link have so that the whole path's reliability is at least 99.9%?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Need r⁴ ≥ 0.999, so r ≥ 0.999^(1/4) ≈ 0.99975.
That means each individual link needs a break probability of only about 1 − 0.99975 = 2.5×10⁻⁴ — much stricter than the overall 10⁻³ target, because failures compound across 4 links.

formulaApplication.question: A link needs 6 nines of reliability. What single break probability does that correspond to?
formulaApplication.explanation:
"n nines" means r = 0.99...9 with n nines, so b = 1 − r = 10⁻ⁿ.
6 nines → b = 10⁻⁶.

theory.question: What does "Peering" mean in the OSI layered model?
options: A) Every layer can talk directly to every other layer
B) Only a layer's peer layer on the other host communicates with it (logically)
C) Only the physical layer can send data
D) It refers to peer-to-peer file sharing protocols
E) Peers must be on the same physical cable
theory.explanation: Peering: layer N on one host only "talks" to layer N on the other host (its peer), even though the data actually travels down through the local stack, across the link, and up the remote stack.

theory.question: What does "Encapsulation" mean in the OSI layered model?
options: A) Each layer removes headers as data moves down the stack
B) Only the top layer adds a header
C) Data is compressed at every layer
D) Each layer adds its own header to the data as it moves down the stack
E) Encapsulation only happens at the physical layer
theory.explanation: As data descends the stack for transmission, each layer wraps it with its own header (and sometimes trailer), building up the frame that finally goes out on the wire. The receiving stack strips these headers back off, layer by layer.

theory.question: In the TCP/IP 5-layer model, which layer sits directly below the Transport layer?
theory.explanation:
Top to bottom: Application, Transport, Network, Link, Physical.
So Network sits directly below Transport, and directly above Link.

theory.question: The lecture asks "Is layering harmful?" What is the main trade-off being pointed at?
options: A) Layering is only a theoretical idea never used in real networks
B) Layering makes networks completely insecure
C) Layering removes the need for addressing
D) Layering doubles the physical cabling needed
E) A clean layered design isn't always the most efficient implementation
theory.explanation: Layering buys simplicity, flexibility and easy incremental change, but strict separation between layers can cost some performance/efficiency compared to a more tightly integrated, non-layered design.

theory.question: The series/parallel/path-based formulas for computing network reliability all rely on which assumption?
options: A) Links never fail, only nodes do
B) Only one link can ever fail at a time
C) Reliability calculations only work for exactly 2 links
D) Each link fails independently of every other link
E) All links have the same reliability
theory.explanation: Every formula (r_series = product of r's, b_parallel = product of b's, and the path-based method for mixed networks) assumes link failures are independent events — that's what allows you to just multiply probabilities together.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY24/25 Q1(3)]
A 640 kbps link carries frames with average length 400 bytes. Assume that the propagation delay is 8 ms, the average frame error probability is 0.2, and a Selective-Reject ARQ is used for error control. What is the minimum window size required to ensure that the throughput is at least 512 kbps, and how many bits would be needed to store the sequence number?
options: A) Window size 5, 5 bits for sequence number
B) Window size 5, 4 bits for sequence number
C) Window size 4, 3 bits for sequence number
D) Window size 4, 2 bits for sequence number
formulaApplication.explanation:
Tframe = 400 × 8 / 640k = 5 ms, a = Tprop/Tframe = 8/5 = 1.6, so 1 + 2a = 4.2
Target U = 512/640 = 0.8. The best SR can ever do is U = 1 − P = 0.8, so we need N ≥ 1 + 2a.
N ≥ 4.2, so N = 5. (Check N = 4: U = 4 × 0.8 / 4.2 = 0.76, too low.)
Selective Reject needs N ≤ 2^(k−1): 5 ≤ 2^(k−1) means k − 1 ≥ 3, so k = 4 bits.
Trap: option A uses the wrong window rule.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY24/25 Q1(4)]
Consider the network shown in Figure Q1.4, what is the minimum transmission rate required between nodes B and C so that the buffers of node B are not flooded, based on the following conditions:
(i) The data rate between A and B is 100 kbps.
(ii) The propagation delay is 20 msec from A to B, and 10 msec from B to C.
(iii) All data frames are 1000 bits long, ACK frames of negligible length.
(iv) The frame error probability is 0.2 from A to B, but 0 from B to C.
(v) A Selective-Reject ARQ protocol is used for both links: the window size is 3 between A and B, and that between B and C is 2.
formulaApplication.explanation:
Idea: B's outgoing throughput must be ≥ its incoming throughput.
A → B: Tframe = 1000/100k = 10 ms, a = 20/10 = 2, 1 + 2a = 5. N = 3 < 5, so
U = N(1 − P)/(1 + 2a) = 3 × 0.8 / 5 = 0.48, and incoming throughput = 0.48 × 100k = 48 kbps.
B → C: need throughput ≥ 48 kbps. At R = 48 kbps: Tframe = 20.8 ms, a = 10/20.8 = 0.48, 1 + 2a = 1.96 ≤ N = 2, so U = 1 and throughput = R.
So the exact minimum is 48 kbps. From the options, 50 kbps is the smallest that works (40 kbps gives only 40 kbps out).

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY23/24 Q1(8)]
The 1 Mbps link between SG and HK has a Round Trip Time (RTT) of 20 milliseconds. The link uses Selective Reject ARQ with a window size of 2. The frame size is 1000 Bytes and the probability of a frame in error is 0.01. Determine the throughput of the link to the nearest Kbps.
formulaApplication.explanation:
Tprop = RTT/2 = 10 ms. Tframe = 8000 bits / 1 Mbps = 8 ms.
a = 10/8 = 1.25, 1 + 2a = 3.5
N = 2 < 3.5, so U = N(1 − P)/(1 + 2a) = 2 × 0.99 / 3.5 = 0.5657
Throughput = 0.5657 × 1 Mbps ≈ 565.7 kbps, closest option 565 Kbps.
Trap: 990 Kbps assumes N ≥ 1 + 2a.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY25/26 Q1(8)]
A 1 Mbps link between NTU and NUS has a Round Trip Time (RTT) of 30 milliseconds. The link uses the Selective ARQ protocol with a window size of 4. Each frame is 1500 Bytes in size. The probability of a frame being in error is 0.05. Determine the throughput of the link (to the nearest 2 decimal point).
formulaApplication.explanation:
Tprop = 15 ms, Tframe = 1500 × 8 / 1 Mbps = 12 ms
a = 15/12 = 1.25, 1 + 2a = 3.5
N = 4 ≥ 3.5, so the window never runs out: U = 1 − P = 0.95
Throughput = 0.95 Mbps.
Trap: 4 × 0.95 / 3.5 = 1.09 > 1, which is why you must check N vs 1 + 2a first.

formulaApplication.question: A 1 Mbps link connects two nodes 20 km apart. Signal speed is 2 × 10⁸ m/s and frames are 1000 bits long. With stop-and-wait flow control and no errors, what is the link utilization?
A sliding window protocol uses window size N = 7 on a link where the normalized propagation delay is a = 5. With no errors, what is the link utilization?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Check N against 1 + 2a = 11. N = 7 < 11, so the window runs out before the first ACK returns.
U = N/(1 + 2a) = 7/11 = 0.636.
Trap: 1.000 only if N ≥ 1 + 2a.

formulaApplication.question: A 100 kbps link carries 500-bit frames with a one-way propagation delay of 12 ms. Using sliding window flow control (no errors), what is the minimum window size for 100% utilization, and the minimum number of sequence number bits?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Tframe = 500/100k = 5 ms, a = 12/5 = 2.4, 1 + 2a = 5.8
U = 1 needs N ≥ 5.8, so N = 6.
Flow control (no errors) rule from the lecture: N ≤ 2^k, so 6 ≤ 2^k gives k = 3.
(With ARQ the rules get stricter: Go-Back-N N ≤ 2^k − 1, Selective Reject N ≤ 2^(k−1).)

formulaApplication.question: A 1 Mbps satellite link has a one-way propagation delay of 270 ms. Frames are 1000 bytes and the sender uses a sliding window of 7 (no errors). What throughput does it achieve?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Tframe = 8000 bits / 1 Mbps = 8 ms
a = 270/8 = 33.75, 1 + 2a = 68.5
N = 7 < 68.5, so U = 7/68.5 = 0.102
Throughput = 0.102 × 1 Mbps ≈ 102 kbps.
Big 'a' links (satellite) need huge windows to be efficient. 14.6 kbps is stop-and-wait (N = 1).

formulaApplication.question: With k = 3 sequence number bits, what are the maximum window sizes for (i) sliding window flow control with no errors, (ii) Go-Back-N ARQ and (iii) Selective Reject ARQ?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Flow control (no errors): N ≤ 2^k = 8
Go-Back-N: N ≤ 2^k − 1 = 7
Selective Reject: N ≤ 2^(k−1) = 4
SR is strictest because the receiver's window must not overlap old and new sequence numbers.

formulaApplication.question: A 10 Mbps link is 5 km long (signal speed 2 × 10⁸ m/s). Frames are 1000 bits and the frame loss probability is 0.05. What is the link utilization with stop-and-wait ARQ?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Tframe = 1000/10⁷ = 100 μs, Tprop = 5000/2 × 10⁸ = 25 μs, a = 0.25
U = (1 − P)/(1 + 2a) = 0.95/1.5 = 0.633.
0.667 ignores errors, and 0.760 uses 1 + a instead of 1 + 2a.

formulaApplication.question: A 2 Mbps link has a one-way propagation delay of 10 ms. It uses Selective Reject ARQ with window size 4, 1000-byte frames and frame error probability 0.1. What is the throughput?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Tframe = 8000/2M = 4 ms, a = 10/4 = 2.5, 1 + 2a = 6
N = 4 < 6, so U = N(1 − P)/(1 + 2a) = 4 × 0.9 / 6 = 0.6
Throughput = 0.6 × 2 Mbps = 1.2 Mbps.
1.8 Mbps wrongly assumes U = 1 − P.

formulaApplication.question: A 50 kbps link carries 50-byte frames with a one-way propagation delay of 14 ms and frame error probability 0.1. It uses Go-Back-N ARQ (as in the lecture, use the Selective Reject utilization formula for Go-Back-N). What is the minimum window size that maximizes utilization, and the minimum number of sequence number bits?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Tframe = 400/50k = 8 ms, a = 14/8 = 1.75, 1 + 2a = 4.5
Max utilization (1 − P = 0.9) needs N ≥ 4.5, so N = 5.
Go-Back-N rule: N ≤ 2^k − 1. 5 ≤ 7, so k = 3 bits.
Trap: 4 bits is the Selective Reject answer (N ≤ 2^(k−1) gives 5 ≤ 8).

formulaApplication.question: A Selective Reject ARQ link has window size N = 3 and normalized propagation delay a = 2. The measured utilization is 0.54. What is the frame error probability P?
formulaApplication.explanation:
1 + 2a = 5 and N = 3 < 5, so U = N(1 − P)/(1 + 2a).
0.54 = 3(1 − P)/5, so 1 − P = 0.9 and P = 0.10.
Trap: 0.46 = 1 − 0.54 assumes U = 1 − P, which only holds when N ≥ 1 + 2a.

theory.question:
[Past Finals AY24/25 Q1(5)]
Consider a data link protocol between A and B with a frame I(i, j) indicating the i-th transmitted frame that demands the j-th frame from the other side. If B receives I(4, 6) and Selective Reject SREJ(6) consecutively from A, what happened to B's previous two frames sent to A?
options: A) I(6, 4) was received by A, but I(7, 4) was lost
B) I(6, 4) was lost, but I(7, 4) was received by A
C) I(4, 6) was received by A, but I(4, 7) was lost
D) I(4, 6) was lost, but I(4, 7) was received by A
theory.explanation:
I(4, 6) from A: A is sending its frame 4 and says 'I want your frame 6 next', so A got B's frames up to 5.
Then SREJ(6): A is rejecting B's frame 6. A only sends SREJ(6) when a LATER frame (7) arrives while 6 is missing.
So B's frame 6 was lost and frame 7 was received.
B's frames carry j = 4 because B still wants A's frame 4 (A's frame 4 hadn't reached B yet). So: I(6, 4) lost, I(7, 4) received.
Options C/D swap i and j. B's own frame number is the first value.

theory.question:
[Past Finals AY23/24 Q1(14)]
The figure below shows the communication between Station A and Station B. Determine the value of I(x,y). THREE bits are used for frame sequencing.
theory.explanation:
B asked for frame 6 with SREJ(6), so A retransmits frame 6: x = 6.
A has received B's frame I(4,6), so the next frame A wants from B is 5: y = 5.
So I(6,5). Trap: I(6,4) forgets that A already got B's frame 4.

theory.question:
[Past Finals AY25/26 Q1(14)]
The figure below shows the communication between Station A and Station B. Determine the value of "x,y" and "w,z". The answer is in the order of x,y,w,z. THREE bits are used for frame sequencing.
theory.explanation:
B's frame I(x,y): A keeps asking for B's frame 4, so x = 4. B got A's frame 5 but frame 6 was lost, so B wants 6: y = 6.
A's frame I(w,z): A has sent 5, 6, 7, and B hasn't sent a SREJ yet, so A sends its next NEW frame, 8 mod 8 = 0 (3-bit numbering): w = 0.
A received B's frame 4, so A now wants 5: z = 5.
Answer 4,6,0,5. Trap: '8' is impossible with 3-bit sequence numbers (0 to 7).

theory.question: What is the main disadvantage of stop-and-wait flow control when the normalized propagation delay a is large?
options: A) The receiver's buffer overflows almost immediately
B) It cannot detect any transmission errors
C) It only works over wireless links
D) It requires a token to be passed around the network
E) The sender must wait a long time before it can send the next frame, so link utilization U = 1/(1+2a) is low
theory.explanation: Two disadvantages: (1) a lost frame/ACK means a long wait until a timeout fires, and (2) with a large a, the sender idles waiting for the ACK, so U = 1/(1+2a) stays low. The fix for (2) is to use buffers at the sender/receiver, i.e. sliding window - that improves the numerator, but 1+2a in the denominator can't be improved.

theory.question: What is the main purpose of flow control at the data link layer?
options: A) To correct bit errors using redundant bits
B) To stop the sender from overwhelming the receiver so its buffers don't overflow
C) To encrypt frames before transmission
D) To choose the best path through the network
E) To decide which station on a shared medium may transmit
theory.explanation:
Flow control = make sure a fast transmitter doesn't overflow the receiver's buffers (assuming no frame errors).
Correcting errors is error control, choosing the path is routing, and sharing the medium is MAC.

theory.question: The ARQ Variants slide splits ARQ into three commonly implemented mechanisms. What are they?
options: A) Stop-and-Wait ARQ, Go-Back-N ARQ, Selective-Reject ARQ
D) Parity Check, CRC, Hamming Code
E) Go-Back-N ARQ, Selective-Reject ARQ, Token Ring
theory.explanation: Just like flow control splits into Stop-and-Wait and Sliding Window (which itself splits into Go-Back-N and Selective-Reject), ARQ mirrors that same tree: Stop-and-Wait ARQ, and the two sliding-window ARQ variants Go-Back-N and Selective-Reject (also called Selective Repeat).

theory.question: In stop-and-wait flow control with binary sequence numbers, the receiver replies ACK1 after receiving a frame. What does ACK1 tell the sender?
options: A) The receiver got f0 correctly and now expects f1
B) The receiver's buffer is full, so stop sending
C) The receiver got f1 correctly and now expects f2
D) The sender should resend both f0 and f1
E) Frame f1 arrived damaged and must be resent
theory.explanation:
ACK n means 'I expect frame n next', so ACK1 implies f0 was received fine.
That's why a 1-bit (binary) sequence number is enough for stop-and-wait.

theory.question: In sliding window flow control, how does the SENDER's window change?
options: A) It shrinks from the trailing edge as ACKs are received, and expands from the leading edge as frames are sent
B) It shrinks from the leading edge as frames are sent, and expands from the trailing edge as ACKs are received
C) It stays a fixed size and slides only when a timeout happens
D) It expands as frames are sent and shrinks as ACKs are received
E) It shrinks from the trailing (left) edge as frames are sent, and expands from the leading (right) edge as ACKs are received
theory.explanation:
Sender: sending frames uses up the window (trailing edge moves right), and ACKs open it up (leading edge moves right).
Receiver works the same way: shrinks as frames are received, expands as ACKs are sent.

theory.question: After receiving F0 and F1, the receiver sends RNR2. What does this mean?
options: A) F0 and F1 were lost, so resend from F0
B) The receiver is ready and the sender may send F2 immediately
C) F2 was received with errors and must be retransmitted
D) F0 and F1 are acknowledged, but the sender must not send more until the receiver sends a normal ACK
E) The ACK is piggybacked on data frame 2
theory.explanation:
RNR = Receive Not Ready. It acknowledges frames (up to 1, expecting 2) while stopping further transmission.
The receiver sends a normal ACK (RR) to let the sender resume.

theory.question: In Stop-and-Wait ARQ, the destination receives a damaged frame. According to the protocol, what can it do?
options: A) It must always send a NAK, discarding is never allowed
B) It must always discard it silently, NAK is never used
C) Either discard it and do nothing, or send a NAK - both are valid variations
D) It forwards the damaged frame up to the network layer anyway
E) It repairs the frame itself using Hamming code
theory.explanation: The protocol explicitly allows two variations on a damaged frame: (1) discard it and rely on the sender's timeout to trigger a retransmit, or (2) send a NAK (negative acknowledgement) so the sender retransmits immediately without waiting for a timeout.

theory.question: In Go-Back-N ARQ, the receiver expects F1 but receives F2 instead. What does the receiver do?
options: A) Accepts F2 and passes it to the higher layer
B) Sends REJ1 (NAK1) and discards F2 and every later frame until F1 arrives correctly
C) Buffers F2 and sends SREJ1 so only F1 is resent
D) Sends ACK3 to skip over the missing frame
E) Does nothing and waits for the sender to time out
theory.explanation:
Go-Back-N accepts frames strictly in sequence (the 'cautious scheme').
Out-of-order frames are discarded, a REJ (NAK) is sent, and the sender goes back and resends F1 and everything after it.
Buffering + SREJ is Selective Reject.

theory.question: Which statement about Selective Reject ARQ is FALSE?
options: A) Only the rejected frames (and timed-out frames) are retransmitted
B) It minimizes retransmissions compared with Go-Back-N
C) The receiver discards out-of-sequence frames, so it needs no extra buffering
D) The receiver tells the sender which frame is bad using SREJ n
E) Frames that arrive after an error are buffered, then put back in order
theory.explanation:
Selective Reject BUFFERS the later frames and reorders them once the missing frame arrives.
That's why it needs more complex buffer management. Discarding is what Go-Back-N does.

theory.question: In the figure, F2 is lost and the receiver replies NAK2 after F3 arrives. If the link uses Go-Back-N ARQ, which frames does the sender retransmit?
options: C) Nothing, it waits for a timeout on F2
E) F0, F1, F2, F3 and F4
theory.explanation:
Go-Back-N: on NAK n, retransmit frame n AND all frames after it, because the receiver threw F3 and F4 away.
'F2 only' is what Selective Reject would do.

theory.question: A and B use I(i, j) frames (i = own sequence number, j = next frame expected from the other side) with Selective Reject and 3-bit sequence numbers. Based on the figure, what is I(x, y)?
theory.explanation:
B sent SREJ(3), so A retransmits frame 3: x = 3.
A received B's frame I(5,3), so A now wants B's frame 6: y = 6.
Same pattern as the past-year I(x,y) questions: first number = what YOU send, second = what you WANT next.

theory.question: Same I(i, j) notation, Selective Reject, 3-bit sequence numbers. B's frame I(1,7) reaches A before any SREJ is sent. What is A's next frame I(w, z)?
theory.explanation:
No SREJ has arrived yet, so A just sends its next NEW frame. A already sent 6, 7, 0, so the next is 1: w = 1.
A received B's frame 1, so A wants B's frame 2: z = 2.
Traps: I(7,2) retransmits too early (A doesn't know 7 was lost yet), and 8 doesn't exist with 3 bits (0 to 7).

formulaApplication.question: A link runs at 2 Mbps. How long does it take to transmit a 4000-bit frame?
formulaApplication.explanation: Tframe = frame length / data rate = 4000 bits / 2×10⁶ bps = 2 ms.

formulaApplication.question: Two nodes are 300 km apart, and the signal travels at 2×10⁸ m/s. What is the one-way propagation delay?
formulaApplication.explanation: Tprop = distance / speed = 300,000 m / 2×10⁸ m/s = 1.5 ms.

formulaApplication.question: A link has Tframe = 2 ms and Tprop = 6 ms. What is the normalized propagation delay a?
formulaApplication.explanation: a = Tprop / Tframe = 6 / 2 = 3.

formulaApplication.question: A link uses stop-and-wait ARQ with frame error probability P = 0.1 and normalized propagation delay a = 2. What is the link utilization?

A 1 Mbps link carries 2000-bit frames using stop-and-wait flow control (no errors). Signal speed is 2×10⁸ m/s. What is the maximum distance between the two nodes so that link utilization stays at least 25%?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Tframe = 2000/10⁶ = 2 ms. Target U = 1/(1+2a) = 0.25 → 1+2a = 4 → a = 1.5.
Tprop = a × Tframe = 1.5 × 2 ms = 3 ms.
Max distance = Tprop × speed = 3 ms × 2×10⁸ m/s = 600,000 m = 600 km.

formulaApplication.question: A sliding window protocol (no errors) achieves 75% utilization with window size N = 6. What is the normalized propagation delay a?
A 500 kbps link carries 1000-bit frames with a one-way propagation delay of 8 ms. It uses Selective-Reject ARQ with window size 4 and frame error probability 0.05. What is the link's throughput?
A Go-Back-N ARQ link has frame error probability P = 0.1 and normalized propagation delay a = 1.75. What is the minimum window size N that achieves at least half of the maximum possible utilization?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Max possible U = 1−P = 0.9, so the target is half of that: 0.45.
1+2a = 4.5. Need N(1−P)/(1+2a) ≥ 0.45 → N×0.9/4.5 ≥ 0.45 → N ≥ 2.25.
Round up: N = 3.

formulaApplication.question: Using 6 sequence-number bits, what is the maximum window size for Go-Back-N ARQ?
formulaApplication.explanation: Go-Back-N rule: N ≤ 2^k − 1 = 2⁶ − 1 = 63.

formulaApplication.question: A link needs a Selective-Reject window of N = 64. What is the minimum number of sequence-number bits required?
formulaApplication.explanation: Selective-Reject rule: N ≤ 2^(k−1). Need 2^(k−1) ≥ 64, so k−1 ≥ 6, k = 7.

formulaApplication.question: A 10 Mbps link achieves 40% utilization. What is the actual throughput?
formulaApplication.explanation: Throughput = U × R = 0.4 × 10 Mbps = 4 Mbps.

formulaApplication.question: A stop-and-wait link with a = 1 is measured to have a utilization of 0.3. What is the frame error probability P?
A 2 Mbps link carries 4000-bit frames between two nodes 400 km apart (signal speed 2×10⁸ m/s). It uses Go-Back-N ARQ with window size 10 and frame error probability 0.02. What is the throughput?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Tframe = 4000/2M = 2 ms. Tprop = 400,000/2×10⁸ = 2 ms. a = 1, so 1+2a = 3.
N = 10 ≥ 3, so the window is more than enough: U caps at 1−P = 0.98.
Throughput = 0.98 × 2 Mbps ≈ 1.96 Mbps.

formulaApplication.question: A Selective-Reject ARQ link has window size N = 3 and error probability P = 0.2. Measured utilization is 0.6. What is the normalized propagation delay a?
A stop-and-wait link (no errors) has a normalized propagation delay a = 0.5. What is the link utilization?
With flow control only (no ARQ) and k = 6 sequence-number bits, what is the maximum window size?
formulaApplication.explanation: Flow-control-only rule: N ≤ 2^k = 2⁶ = 64.

formulaApplication.question: A Go-Back-N ARQ link needs a window size of at least 100. What is the minimum number of sequence-number bits?

A satellite link has a huge normalized propagation delay a = 125. It uses Selective-Reject ARQ with an 8-bit sequence number field (maximum allowed window) and negligible frame errors. What is the link utilization?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Max window for 8-bit SR: N ≤ 2^(8−1) = 128.
1+2a = 1+250 = 251. U = N(1−P)/(1+2a) ≈ 128/251 ≈ 0.51.
Even the largest window your sequence-number bits allow can't fully hide a huge satellite-scale 'a' — this is exactly why real satellite links often need extra tricks beyond just widening the window.

formulaApplication.question: A 64 kbps link carries 128-byte frames with a one-way propagation delay corresponding to a = 0.3125, using Selective-Reject ARQ with window 8 and error probability 0.1. What is the utilization?
formulaApplication.explanation:
1+2a = 1+0.625 = 1.625. Best possible U = 1−P = 0.9.
Check window: N(1−P)/(1+2a) = 8×0.9/1.625 ≈ 4.43, far more than 0.9, so the window isn't the bottleneck.
U = min(0.9, 4.43) = 0.9.

formulaApplication.question: A 1 Mbps link carries 12,000-bit frames using stop-and-wait flow control (no errors). What one-way propagation delay gives a link utilization of exactly 80%?

theory.question: In sliding window flow control, how does the RECEIVER's window change?
options: A) It only changes when a timeout occurs
B) It shrinks as ACKs are sent and expands as frames are received
C) It never changes size once set
D) It shrinks from the trailing edge as frames are received, and expands from the leading edge as ACKs are sent
E) It always mirrors the sender's window exactly frame for frame
theory.explanation: Symmetric to the sender's window: the receiver's window shrinks (trailing edge moves right) as frames come in, and expands (leading edge moves right) as it sends ACKs back.

theory.question: In Stop-and-Wait ARQ, the source sends a frame, but the ACK gets damaged in transit. What happens?
options: A) The source immediately sends the next frame anyway
B) The destination automatically sends a fresh ACK
C) The destination re-sends the original frame back to the source
E) The source doesn't recognize the damaged ACK, times out, and retransmits the same frame; the destination gets two copies and discards one
theory.explanation: A damaged ACK looks like no ACK at all to the source, so its timeout fires and it resends the frame. The destination then has two copies of the same frame and simply discards the duplicate.

theory.question: What is the purpose of the retransmission timer in ARQ schemes?
options: A) To trigger a retransmission if an expected ACK never arrives (frame or ACK was lost)
B) To measure the round-trip time for statistics only
C) To decide which station may access the medium
D) To encrypt frames before sending
E) To slow down the sender so it never overwhelms the receiver
theory.explanation: Without a timer, a lost frame or a lost ACK would leave the sender waiting forever. The timeout guarantees the sender eventually gives up waiting and retransmits.

theory.question: In Go-Back-N ARQ, under what condition does the receiver accept a frame?
options: A) Only if it arrives strictly in the expected sequence order
B) Any frame is accepted and reordered later
C) Only if it is error-free, regardless of sequence order
D) Only the very first frame of a session is checked for sequence
E) If it arrives within the receiver's open window, even out of order
theory.explanation: Go-Back-N's receiver is the "cautious" scheme: any out-of-sequence frame is discarded outright, even if it isn't damaged, and the sender must go back and resend from the missing frame onward.

theory.question: In Selective-Reject ARQ, under what condition does the receiver accept a frame?
options: A) Only if it arrives strictly in sequence
B) Never — Selective-Reject only ever discards frames
C) Only if the window is completely full
D) If it falls within the receiver's currently open window, even if it arrives out of sequence
E) Only the first and last frames of a batch are accepted
theory.explanation: Unlike Go-Back-N, Selective-Reject buffers out-of-order frames that fall inside its open window, then reorders them once the missing frame(s) finally arrive — this is what lets it avoid re-sending frames that already arrived fine.

theory.question: In the figure, F6 is lost and the receiver replies NAK6 only after F8 has already arrived. If the link uses Go-Back-N ARQ, which frames does the sender retransmit?
options: C) Nothing — it waits for a timeout
E) F5, F6, F7 and F8
theory.explanation: Go-Back-N: on NAK n, the sender goes back and resends frame n and every frame sent after it, since the receiver discarded F7 and F8 (they arrived out of sequence while F6 was still missing).

theory.question: A and B use I(i, j) frames (i = own sequence number, j = next frame expected from the other side), Selective Reject, 3-bit sequence numbers. Based on the figure, what is I(x, y)?
theory.explanation:
B sent SREJ(2), so A retransmits frame 2: x = 2.
A received B's frame I(4,2), so A now wants B's frame 5 next: y = 5.

theory.question: Which of the following correctly pairs each protocol with its maximum window size given k sequence-number bits?
options: A) All three protocols share the same maximum window size, 2^k
B) Flow control (no errors): 2^k, Go-Back-N: 2^k − 1, Selective-Reject: 2^(k−1)
C) Selective-Reject always allows the largest window of the three
D) Flow control (no errors): 2^(k−1), Go-Back-N: 2^k, Selective-Reject: 2^k − 1
E) Flow control (no errors): 2^k − 1, Go-Back-N: 2^k, Selective-Reject: 2^(k−1)
theory.explanation: From loosest to strictest: plain flow control has no ambiguity to avoid so N ≤ 2^k; Go-Back-N reserves one sequence number to detect a full wraparound so N ≤ 2^k − 1; Selective-Reject needs to tell old vs new frames apart while buffering out-of-order ones, so it's capped at half the space, N ≤ 2^(k−1).

theory.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer?
options: A) Assembling data into a frame with address and error detection fields
B) Disassembling frames, including address recognition and error detection
C) Offering several MAC options for the same LLC
D) Providing flow and error control as the interface to higher layers
E) Governing access to the transmission medium
theory.explanation:
MAC: frame assembly (address + error detection fields), disassembly (address recognition, error detection) and governing medium access.
Interface to higher levels with flow/error control is the LLC's job.

theory.question: Which of the following is a function MAC has that is NOT found in traditional Layer 2 Data Link Control?
options: A) Detecting errors in a frame
B) Governing access to the transmission medium
E) Assembling data into a frame
theory.explanation: The slide calls this out specifically: governing access to the shared transmission medium is a MAC job with no equivalent in classic (pre-802) Layer 2 data link control, which only had framing, addressing and error detection.

theory.question: Which of the following is a DISADVANTAGE of making MAC decisions centrally rather than in a distributed way?
options: A) It causes coordination problems between stations
B) It needs complex access logic at every station
C) It gives less control over access
D) It can only use asynchronous (dynamic) allocation
E) It creates a single point of failure and a potential bottleneck
theory.explanation:
Central MAC pros: greater control, simple station logic, avoids coordination problems.
Central MAC cons: single point of failure, potential bottleneck.

theory.question: The MAC Decision Making Options are organized around two questions. What are they?
options: A) When (early vs. late) and Why (cost vs. performance)
B) Where (LAN vs. WAN) and How (wired vs. wireless)
C) How (static vs. dynamic) and Why (reliability vs. speed)
D) Where (central vs. distributed) and How (synchronous/static vs. asynchronous/dynamic)
E) Who (sender vs. receiver) and What (data vs. control)
theory.explanation: "Where?" splits into central vs. distributed control; "How?" splits into synchronous (static) vs. asynchronous (dynamic) allocation. Every other MAC design question in this section falls under one of these two.

theory.question: In MAC design, what does a synchronous (static) solution mean?
options: A) Stations contend and risk collisions
B) A token is passed around a ring
C) Stations reserve the channel only when they have data
D) Capacity is given out in response to demand
E) A specific capacity is dedicated to each connection
theory.explanation: Synchronous/static = fixed capacity per connection, decided ahead of time regardless of whether the station actually has data to send.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY24/25 Q1(6)]
Consider an Ethernet LAN with 100Mbps data rate, it requires:
(i) Maximum cable length per segment is 200 meters and the propagation delay is 1 μsec per 100 meters.
(ii) A repeater used to connect two segments (thus to extend the LAN size) causes an extra delay of 3 μsec.
(iii) Maximum 5 repeaters can be deployed between any two stations.
What is the minimum frame size required for properly operating this LAN?
formulaApplication.explanation:
5 repeaters connect 6 segments.
One-way worst case τ = 6 × 200 m × (1 μs/100 m) + 5 × 3 μs = 12 + 15 = 27 μs
Frame must last ≥ 2τ = 54 μs
Min frame = 54 μs × 100 Mbps = 5400 bits.
Trap: using 5 segments gives 2 × 25 = 50 μs = 5000 bits.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY24/25 Q1(7)]
Consider an Ethernet LAN where four stations are connected to a hub, and the distance between each station and the Ethernet hub is the same. Assume that a collision has just happened (causing the Binary Exponential Backoff, or BEB, to kick in), what is the probability that the next event on the channel is a successful transmission?
formulaApplication.explanation:
1st retry: each station picks K ∈ {0, 1}, each with probability 1/2.
The next event happens in slot 0 unless nobody picks 0.
• Exactly one station picks 0: 4 × (1/2)⁴ = 4/16 → success ✓
• Two or more pick 0: collision
• Nobody picks 0 (1/16): all 4 go in slot 1 → collision
P(next event is success) = 4/16 = 1/4.
(Tutorial 3 hint: an empty slot doesn't count as an event.)

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY24/25 Q1(8)]
Given the same conditions as the previous question (four stations on a hub, a collision has just happened), but assuming each of the four stations (A, B, C, D) can configure their probabilities of transmitting in the future time slots 0 and 1. Which of the following configuration would maximize the throughput?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Count expected successful slots out of slots 0 and 1:
A) all 4 always in slot 0 → guaranteed collision → 0
B) 4 stations in slot 0 at p = 0.5: P(exactly one) = 4 × 0.5⁴ = 0.25, slot 1 unused → 0.25
C) A, B always in slot 0 and C, D always in slot 1 → both slots collide → 0
D) slot 0: P(exactly one of A, B) = 2 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.5; slot 1 same = 0.5 → total 1.0 ✓
Splitting stations across slots and using p = 1/(stations in that slot) maximizes throughput.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY23/24 Q1(6)]
Station A, Station B and Station C, use 0.2-persistent slotted-ALOHA Medium Access Control protocol. They both have one packet of data to transmit at time t=0+c, where c is a small value less that one slot time. Determine the probability that one of the stations transmit successfully at the next time slot, i.e. t=1.
formulaApplication.explanation:
Success = exactly one of the 3 stations transmits.
Pr(S) = N p (1 − p)^(N−1) = 3 × 0.2 × 0.8² = 0.384.
Traps: 0.512 = 0.8³ (nobody transmits), 0.008 = 0.2³ (all transmit), 0.128 = one specific station only.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY23/24 Q1(7)]
Three stations in a CSMA/CD network were involved in a collision when they try to transmit at the same time. Determine the probability that the next event in the first retry is a successful transmission of a frame.
formulaApplication.explanation:
First retry: each picks K ∈ {0, 1} with probability 1/2.
Next event is a success only if exactly one station picks slot 0: 3 × (1/2)³ = 3/8 = 0.375.
If nobody picks 0 (1/8), all three go in slot 1 and collide. Two or more in slot 0 also collide.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY23/24 Q1(9)]
The CSMA/CD network has a minimum frame size of 512 bits. The worst case 1-way delay in the largest single network is 8 microseconds. Determine the maximum transmission rate that can be used on the CSMA/CD network.
formulaApplication.explanation:
Rule: Tframe ≥ 2τ, i.e. frame size / R ≥ 2 × one-way delay.
R ≤ 512 / (2 × 8 μs) = 512 / 16 μs = 32 Mbps.
Trap: 64 Mbps would come from forgetting the ×2 round trip (not an option, but a common slip).

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY25/26 Q1(6)]
In a radio communication system, multiple ground stations need to send data using the slotted ALOHA Medium Access Control protocol. Two ground stations, station A and station B, each have one data packet ready to transmit in the next time slot. Each station will attempt to transmit its packet in the upcoming time slot with a probability of 0.2. If a collision occurs, the stations will attempt to retransmit in subsequent slots following the same procedure. What is the probability that NO station is able to successfully transmits its packet in the next TWO time slot?
formulaApplication.explanation:
P(success in one slot) = exactly one transmits = 2 × 0.2 × 0.8 = 0.32, so P(no success) = 0.68.
No success in slot 1 means both still have packets, so slot 2 is the same situation.
P(no success in 2 slots) = 0.68² = 0.4624, not listed → E.
Traps: 0.64 = 0.8² (nobody transmits in 1 slot), 0.4096 = 0.8⁴ (nobody transmits in either slot). Those miss the collision case.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY25/26 Q1(7)]
In a CSMA/CD network, three stations (A, B and C) simultaneously attempt to transmit, resulting in a collision. They use a binary exponential backoff algorithm to resolve the collision. What is the probability that station A successfully transmits its frame in the first retry?
formulaApplication.explanation:
First retry: each picks slot 0 or 1 with probability 1/2. A succeeds if nobody else is in A's slot.
A = 0, B = 1, C = 1: (1/2)³ = 1/8
A = 1, B = 0, C = 0: (1/2)³ = 1/8 (B and C collide in slot 0, A is alone in slot 1)
Total = 1/4 = 0.25.
Note: there's no official answer key. This uses the lecture's slot-by-slot BEB model (slide 27). 0.125 only counts A winning slot 0, and 0.375 is 'ANY station succeeds first'.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY25/26 Q1(9)]
A CSMA/CD network operates at a data rate of 10 Mbps. The propagation speed of signals in the medium is 2 × 10⁸ meters per second. The minimum frame size is 500 bits. The maximum number of repeaters between two stations is 1, connecting two network segments. The repeater has a delay of 2 microseconds. Determine the maximum network segment length, all of equal size.
formulaApplication.explanation:
Tframe = 500 / 10 Mbps = 50 μs, and Tframe ≥ 2τ, so τ ≤ 25 μs (one-way).
One-way path = 2 segments + 1 repeater: 2L / (2 × 10⁸) + 2 μs ≤ 25 μs
2L ≤ 23 μs × 2 × 10⁸ = 4600 m, so L ≤ 2300 m, not listed → E.
Trap: ignoring the repeater delay gives 2500 m (option B).

formulaApplication.question: A slotted ALOHA network has 4 nodes and each transmits in a slot with probability p = 0.25. What is the probability that a slot is successful?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Pr(S) = N p (1 − p)^(N−1) = 4 × 0.25 × 0.75³ = 0.422.
0.105 is just one specific node succeeding (p(1 − p)³), and 0.316 = 0.75⁴ is an empty slot.

formulaApplication.question: A pure ALOHA network has 3 nodes, each transmitting with probability p = 0.1 per frame time. What is the probability of a successful transmission?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Pure ALOHA: nobody else may start in the frame-time before OR after, so the exponent doubles.
Pr(S) = N p (1 − p)^(2N−2) = 3 × 0.1 × 0.9⁴ = 0.197.
0.243 = 3 × 0.1 × 0.9² is the slotted ALOHA answer.

formulaApplication.question: In slotted ALOHA, 3 nodes each transmit in a slot with probability 0.4. What is the probability that the slot ends in a collision?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Every slot is Empty, Success or Collision.
Empty = 0.6³ = 0.216
Success = 3 × 0.4 × 0.6² = 0.432
Collision = 1 − 0.216 − 0.432 = 0.352.
0.064 = 0.4³ only counts all three colliding.

formulaApplication.question: A slotted ALOHA network has N = 5 nodes that always have frames to send. Which transmission probability p maximizes throughput, and what is that maximum?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Pr(S) = N p (1 − p)^(N−1). Differentiate and set to 0: p* = 1/N = 0.2.
Pr(S) = 5 × 0.2 × 0.8⁴ = 0.4096 ≈ 0.410.
0.368 = 1/e is the limit as N → ∞, not the exact value for N = 5.

formulaApplication.question: At an offered load of G = 0.5 frames per frame time (large number of nodes), what are the throughputs of slotted and pure ALOHA?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Slotted: G e^(−G) = 0.5 × e^(−0.5) = 0.303
Pure: G e^(−2G) = 0.5 × e^(−1) = 0.184 (pure ALOHA's peak is at G = 0.5).

formulaApplication.question: A 10 Mbps CSMA/CD LAN has a maximum one-way propagation delay of 25.6 μs. What is the minimum frame size?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Tframe ≥ 2τ = 51.2 μs
Min frame = 51.2 μs × 10 Mbps = 512 bits (= 64 bytes, Ethernet's minimum).
256 bits forgets the round trip.

formulaApplication.question: Two Ethernet stations A and B keep colliding. They are now on their 3rd retrial under BEB. What is the probability that they collide again?
formulaApplication.explanation:
3rd retrial: K ∈ {0, …, 7}, 8 choices each.
Collide if both pick the same K: 8 × (1/8)(1/8) = 1/8 = 0.125.
Pattern from the slide: 1st retrial 0.5, 2nd 0.25, 3rd 0.125.

formulaApplication.question: A 50 Mbps CSMA/CD LAN has segments of up to 300 m (signal speed 2 × 10⁸ m/s). At most 3 repeaters sit between any two stations, each adding 4 μs. What is the minimum frame size?
formulaApplication.explanation:
3 repeaters connect 4 segments.
One-way τ = 4 × 300 / 2 × 10⁸ + 3 × 4 μs = 6 + 12 = 18 μs
2τ = 36 μs → min frame = 36 μs × 50 Mbps = 1800 bits (225 bytes).
1500 bits uses 3 segments, 900 bits forgets the round trip.

formulaApplication.question: After a collision, stations A and B use a modified backoff: each retransmits in slot 0 or slot 1. A picks slot 0 with probability 1/4 and B picks slot 0 with probability 1/2. What is the probability that the first event on the channel is a success? (An empty slot is not an event.)
formulaApplication.explanation:
Slot 0 cases:
• Only A in slot 0: 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8 → success
• Only B in slot 0: 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8 → success
• Both in slot 0: 1/8 → collision
• Neither: 3/8 → both go in slot 1 → collision
P(first event is success) = 1/8 + 3/8 = 1/2.
(Same idea as Tutorial 3 Q3.)

theory.question: What are the maximum throughputs of slotted ALOHA and pure ALOHA (for a large number of nodes)?
theory.explanation:
Slotted: Pr(S) = G e^(−G), max 1/e at G = 1.
Pure: Pr(S) = G e^(−2G), max 1/(2e) at G = 0.5.
Pure ALOHA is worse because a frame can partly overlap frames sent up to 1 frame-time before OR after it.

theory.question: A CSMA station senses the medium busy, keeps listening until it becomes idle, then transmits immediately with probability 1. If two stations become ready at the same time, a collision is guaranteed. Which variant is this?
theory.explanation:
1-persistent = 'selfish': jumps in the moment the medium is idle.
Non-persistent waits a random time when busy ('deferential'). p-persistent transmits with probability p in each slot when idle ('wise guy').

theory.question: What is the vulnerable time for CSMA?
options: A) Twice the frame transmission time
theory.explanation:
A collision can only happen if another station starts before it can hear the first transmission, i.e. within the max propagation time.
So longer propagation delay means worse CSMA performance.

theory.question: In CSMA/CD, what is the worst-case time for a sender to detect a collision (a = maximum propagation delay)?
options: A) The time to send a 48-bit jam signal
D) One slot time of the backoff
theory.explanation:
Worst case: the other station starts just before A's signal reaches it (time a), and its signal takes another a to come back.
Total 2a, which is exactly why Ethernet's frame must last at least the round-trip time.

theory.question: Which of the following is NOT a disadvantage of slotted ALOHA?
options: A) A single active node can transmit continuously at the full channel rate
B) Some slots are left empty
D) Throughput is capped at about 37%
theory.explanation:
That's one of its PROS (also: highly decentralized, simple).
Cons: collisions, empty slots, clock synchronization (and the 1/e cap).

theory.question: Which of the following Ethernet destination addresses is a MULTICAST address?
theory.explanation:
Look at the SECOND hex digit from the left (the first byte's lowest bit).
Odd → multicast, even → unicast, all F's → broadcast.
01: '1' is odd → multicast. 4A, 2C, 08 are even → unicast. FF…FF is broadcast.

theory.question: How many collision domains and broadcast domains are there in the network shown?
theory.explanation:
Collision domains (switches and routers break them, hubs don't):
• Switch side: each switch port is its own domain, 3 PCs + the switch–router link = 4
• Hub side: the hub, its 3 PCs and the hub–router link are all ONE domain = 1
Total 5.
Broadcast domains: only the router splits them, so 2 (one per router interface).

theory.question: In the network shown (no routers), how many collision domains and broadcast domains are there?
theory.explanation:
Each switch port = 1 collision domain. The switch has 4 ports in use:
• Port to Hub A (Hub A + its 3 PCs share it) = 1
• Port to Hub B (Hub B + its 2 PCs) = 1
• 2 PCs plugged directly into the switch = 2
Total 4.
Switches and hubs forward broadcasts, so everything is 1 broadcast domain.

theory.question: Why must an Ethernet (10 Mbps) frame be at least 64 bytes long?
options: A) Because the preamble alone is 64 bytes
B) So the sender is still transmitting when a collision from the far end (up to 51.2 μs round trip) comes back
C) To reduce the 9.6 μs gap between frames
D) So that the jam signal fits inside the frame
E) Because the CRC field needs at least 64 bytes to work
theory.explanation:
802.3 sets max round trip 2τ = 51.2 μs (about 2500 m). At 10 Mbps, 51.2 μs = 512 bits = 64 bytes.
64 B = 14 B header + 46 B data + 4 B CRC, with padding if data < 46 B.

theory.question: Which statement about Ethernet's Binary Exponential Backoff is correct?
options: A) The station never gives up retrying
B) The delay is fixed so that stations retransmit in lock step
C) K is chosen from {0, 1, …, n} after the n-th collision
D) After the n-th collision, K is chosen from {0, 1, …, 2ⁿ − 1} and the delay is K × 51.2 μs, with K capped at 1023
E) After every collision, K is always chosen from {0, 1}
theory.explanation:
1st collision: K ∈ {0,1}, 2nd: {0,…,3}, n-th: {0,…,2ⁿ−1}, max K = 1023, give up after about 16 tries.
Randomness stops stations retransmitting in lock step, and the growing range copes with many hosts.

formulaApplication.question: A CSMA/CD network runs at 20 Mbps with a worst-case one-way propagation delay of 20 μs. What is the minimum frame size?
formulaApplication.explanation: Lmin = 2τ × R = 2 × 20 μs × 20 Mbps = 800 bits.

formulaApplication.question: A 100 Mbps Ethernet LAN has a total one-way propagation delay of 3 μs. What is the minimum frame size?
formulaApplication.explanation: Lmin = 2τ × R = 2 × 3 μs × 100 Mbps = 600 bits.

formulaApplication.question: A 10 Mbps CSMA/CD LAN connects two segments of 500 m each (propagation 2 μs per 100 m) through a single repeater that adds 5 μs of delay. What is the minimum frame size?
formulaApplication.explanation:
τ = 2 segments × 500 m × (2 μs/100 m) + 1 repeater × 5 μs = 20 μs + 5 μs = 25 μs.
Lmin = 2 × 25 μs × 10 Mbps = 500 bits.

formulaApplication.question: A CSMA/CD LAN requires a minimum frame size of 1000 bits and runs at 20 Mbps. What is the maximum one-way propagation delay this network can tolerate?
A CSMA/CD network has a minimum frame size of 512 bits and a worst-case one-way propagation delay of 12.8 μs. What is the maximum data rate this network can run at?
Two stations are involved in a collision on an Ethernet segment. On their 4th collision (4th retry), what is the probability they collide again?
formulaApplication.explanation:
After the n-th collision, K is chosen from {0,...,2ⁿ−1}: for the 4th collision, that's 16 slots.
Two stations collide again only if they pick the SAME slot: 16 × (1/16)² = 1/16.

formulaApplication.question: 5 stations on an Ethernet segment collide simultaneously. On their first retry (each picks slot 0 or 1), what is the probability that exactly one station succeeds?
formulaApplication.explanation: P(exactly one succeeds) = n / 2ⁿ = 5 / 2⁵ = 5/32.

formulaApplication.question: 6 stations collide simultaneously on an Ethernet segment. What is the probability that exactly one station succeeds on the first retry?
formulaApplication.explanation: P(exactly one succeeds) = n / 2ⁿ = 6 / 2⁶ = 6/64 = 3/32.

formulaApplication.question: In a slotted ALOHA network, 5 stations each transmit with probability p = 0.2 in a given slot. What is the probability of a successful transmission in that slot?
In slotted ALOHA, 3 stations each transmit with probability p = 0.4 per slot. What is the probability of a collision in a given slot?
In pure ALOHA, 2 stations each transmit with probability p = 0.3 per frame-time. What is the probability of a successful transmission?
formulaApplication.explanation: Pure ALOHA: P(success) = N·p·(1−p)^(2N−2) = 2 × 0.3 × 0.7² ≈ 0.294.

formulaApplication.question: A slotted ALOHA network has 8 stations that always have data ready. What value of p maximizes throughput, and what is that maximum throughput?
At an offered load of G = 2 frames per frame-time (large number of nodes), what are the throughputs of slotted and pure ALOHA?
A CSMA/CD LAN has 6 cable segments of 150 m each (propagation 1 μs per 100 m), joined by 5 repeaters each adding 2.5 μs of delay. The LAN runs at 50 Mbps. What is the minimum frame size?

Two stations keep colliding under Binary Exponential Backoff. What is the probability that they are STILL colliding after their first two retries combined (i.e. they collide on both the 1st AND 2nd retry)?
formulaApplication.explanation:
1st retry: window = 2, P(collide again) = 1/2.
2nd retry: window = 4, P(collide again) = 1/4.
Both must happen: 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.

formulaApplication.question: In slotted ALOHA with 6 stations each transmitting with probability p = 0.15 per slot, what is the probability of a successful transmission?

A CSMA/CD network requires a minimum frame size of 200 bits and runs at 10 Mbps. Cable segments are 200 m each (propagation 1 μs per 100 m), and each repeater between segments adds 2 μs of delay. How many repeaters are used between the two farthest stations?
formulaApplication.explanation:
τ budget = Lmin/(2R) = 200/(2×10×10⁶) = 10 μs.
Each 200 m segment contributes 200×(1μs/100m) = 2 μs of propagation delay. With n repeaters there are (n+1) segments, so τ = (n+1)×2 μs (segments) + n×2 μs (repeaters) = (4n+2) μs.
Solve: 4n+2 = 10 → n = 2 repeaters.

formulaApplication.question: In pure ALOHA with a large number of nodes, what p maximizes throughput for N = 10 stations, and what is that maximum throughput?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Optimal p = 1/N = 0.1.
Pr(S) = 10 × 0.1 × 0.9¹⁸ ≈ 0.150 (pure ALOHA's exponent is 2N−2 = 18).

formulaApplication.question: A 640 kbps trunk carries phone calls at 64 kbps each. How many simultaneous calls can it support?
formulaApplication.explanation: 640 kbps / 64 kbps per call = 10 calls.

formulaApplication.question: A 4 Mbps CSMA/CD LAN has segments joined so that the worst-case one-way propagation delay is 100 μs. What is the minimum frame size, and roughly how many bytes is that?
formulaApplication.explanation: Lmin = 2τR = 2 × 100 μs × 4 Mbps = 800 bits = 100 bytes.

theory.question: A CSMA station senses the medium is busy, then waits a RANDOM amount of time before sensing again (rather than continuously monitoring). Which CSMA variant is this?
theory.explanation: Non-persistent ('deferential') CSMA backs off for a random time when it senses the medium busy, rather than waiting right at the edge of the transmission the way 1-persistent does.

theory.question: A CSMA station senses the medium is idle and, in each time slot, transmits with a fixed probability p (otherwise it waits for the next slot). Which CSMA variant is this?
theory.explanation: p-persistent ('wise guy') CSMA: on finding the channel idle, transmit with probability p in each slot, and defer with probability 1−p, repeating slot by slot until it transmits.

theory.question: In the network shown, a router connects two switches, each with 3 PCs plugged directly into it. How many collision domains and broadcast domains are there?
theory.explanation:
Each switch port is its own collision domain: 3 PCs + the uplink to the router, on each of the 2 switches = 4 + 4 = 8 collision domains.
Only the router splits broadcast domains, and there's one on each side of it, so 2 broadcast domains.

theory.question: Which of the following Ethernet destination addresses is the BROADCAST address?
theory.explanation:
All 48 bits set to 1 (FF in every byte) is the reserved broadcast address, delivered to every station on the LAN.
An odd second hex digit (like 01, or 0C is even, 42 is even, etc.) signals multicast; broadcast is the special all-ones case.

theory.question: In CSMA/CD, what is the purpose of the jam signal sent immediately after a collision is detected?
options: A) To repair the corrupted frame automatically
B) To increase the transmission rate temporarily
C) To make sure every station on the segment notices the collision and stops transmitting
D) To encrypt the colliding frames
E) To identify which station caused the collision
theory.explanation: A brief jam signal is sent right after a collision is detected, ensuring all transmitting stations definitely notice the collision (even ones that might have just barely missed sensing it) and abort, before everyone enters backoff.

theory.question: What is the purpose of Ethernet's minimum interframe gap (9.6 μs at 10 Mbps)?
options: A) To give receivers time to reset and prepare for the next frame, and let the medium settle between frames
B) To act as the jam signal
C) To pad short frames up to the minimum size
D) To encode the destination address
E) To allow time for collision detection during transmission
theory.explanation: The interframe gap is idle time deliberately left between consecutive frames so receiving stations have time to process the previous frame and the physical medium can settle before the next transmission begins.

theory.question: Why was CSMA/CD developed as an improvement over plain ALOHA?
options: A) CSMA/CD removes the need for a minimum frame size
B) Sensing the channel before transmitting, and aborting immediately on collision, avoids wasting the whole frame time on doomed transmissions
C) CSMA/CD works only on wireless networks
D) CSMA/CD eliminates the need for any frame addressing
E) CSMA/CD guarantees zero collisions can ever occur
theory.explanation: Plain ALOHA transmits blindly with no regard for other traffic. CSMA adds "listen before talking," and CSMA/CD adds "listen WHILE talking" so a collision is detected and transmission aborted early, rather than wasting the full frame time the way ALOHA does.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY24/25 Q1(9)]
Consider a Wi-Fi network modeled by the multi-access reservation protocol (MARP). It has a data rate of 10 Mbps, and the length of the data frame is 1000 bits, in addition to another 10 data bits carried by the reservation frame. In order to achieve a throughput beyond 90%, what should be the link utilization achieved by the MAC protocol used for the first contention (reservation) phase?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Useful bits per cycle = 1000 + 10 = 1010 (the reservation frame carries data too).
Window = data frame + expected reservation time = 1000 + 10/Sr.
S = 1010 / (1000 + 10/Sr) ≥ 0.9
1000 + 10/Sr ≤ 1122.2, so 10/Sr ≤ 122.2 and Sr ≥ 10/122.2 = 9/110.
(This matches the slide formula S = u/((u − v) + v/Sr) with u = 1010, v = 10.)

formulaApplication.question: A LAN uses MARP. The reservation frame is 10 ms long and carries no data bits. The data frame is 2 s long. The reservation-phase MAC protocol has utilization 0.4. What is the MARP utilization?
formulaApplication.explanation:
No data in the reservation frame: S = u / (u + v/Sr)
u = 2 s, v = 0.01 s, Sr = 0.4
S = 2 / (2 + 0.025) = 0.988.
0.995 uses v instead of v/Sr (forgets the failed trials).

formulaApplication.question: A Wi-Fi network uses MARP at 2 Mbps. The data frame is 1000 bits long, of which 10 information bits are carried in the reservation frame. The reservation-phase MAC protocol has utilization 0.5. What is the throughput?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Reservation frame carries data: S = u / ((u − v) + v/Sr)
u = 1000, v = 10, Sr = 0.5
S = 1000 / (990 + 20) = 0.990
Throughput = 0.990 × 2 Mbps ≈ 1.98 Mbps.
1.96 Mbps uses the 'no data in reservation' formula (1000/1020).

formulaApplication.question: MARP uses slotted ALOHA (running at its maximum utilization) in the reservation phase. The data frame is 500 bits and the reservation frame is 20 bits with no data. What is the best MARP utilization achievable?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Max slotted ALOHA utilization Sr = 1/e ≈ 0.368.
S = u / (u + v/Sr) = 500 / (500 + 20e) = 500 / 554.4 ≈ 0.902.
0.822 would be using pure ALOHA (Sr = 1/(2e)).

formulaApplication.question: In MARP, the data frame takes 1 ms, each reservation trial frame takes 0.1 ms, and the reservation-phase utilization is Sr = 0.25. What is the average length of a full transmission window?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Expected trials = 1/Sr = 4, so reservation takes 4 × 0.1 = 0.4 ms on average.
Window = u + v/Sr = 1 + 0.4 = 1.4 ms.

formulaApplication.question: MARP has a 1000-bit data frame and a 20-bit reservation frame that carries no data. What is the minimum reservation-phase utilization Sr needed for MARP utilization of at least 0.95?
formulaApplication.explanation:
S = 1000 / (1000 + 20/Sr) ≥ 0.95
1000 + 20/Sr ≤ 1052.6, so 20/Sr ≤ 52.6 and Sr ≥ 0.38.
Same reverse-solving trick as the past-year MARP question.

theory.question: The figure shows one MARP cycle. What is the correct description of the two phases?
options: A) Phase 1: RTS/CTS handshake. Phase 2: collision detection
B) Phase 1: stations send data frames. Phase 2: the AP sends ACKs
C) Phase 1: stations send reservation trials until one succeeds. Phase 2: that station transmits its data frame
D) Both phases are contention-free polling
E) Phase 1: data transmission. Phase 2: channel reservation for the next cycle
theory.explanation:
MARP = 2-phase protocol:
Phase 1 (reservation): contend with short trial frames (length v) using some MAC protocol until one succeeds.
Phase 2 (transmission): the winner sends its data frame (length u) with no collisions.

theory.question: In MARP, the MAC protocol used in the reservation phase has utilization Sr. What is the expected number of reservation trial frames per cycle?
theory.explanation:
Each trial succeeds with probability Sr, so P(X = k) = Sr(1 − Sr)^(k−1), a geometric distribution with E[X] = 1/Sr.
So the average transmission window is u + v/Sr.

theory.question: In the MARP transmission-window diagram, what do "u units of time" and "v units of time" represent?
options: A) u = the whole cycle length; v = the utilization Sr
B) u = propagation delay; v = processing delay
C) u = one reservation trial time; v = the data frame's transmission time
D) u = the data frame's transmission time (Phase 2); v = the time for one reservation trial (Phase 1)
E) u and v are both reservation trial times
theory.explanation: The MARP Transmission Window diagram labels Phase 2 (Transmission) as lasting u units of time, and each little reservation trial mark in Phase 1 as lasting v units of time.

theory.question: In the MARP reservation-phase flowchart, what happens when a reservation Trial fails (the "N" branch)?
options: A) The reservation phase ends and Phase 2 starts immediately
B) The whole cycle aborts and no station gets to transmit
C) The station transmits its data frame anyway
D) The station loops back and attempts another reservation trial
E) The station switches to CSMA/CD
theory.explanation: The flowchart's Trial diamond feeds back into itself on "N" (failure) - the station keeps retrying reservation trials until one succeeds ("Y"), only then moving down to "Transmit data frame". This retry loop is exactly why the number of trials X follows a geometric distribution with E[X] = 1/Sr.

theory.question: How is MARP's utilization S formally defined?
options: B) S = Time for message transmission / Transmission window
C) S = Number of reservation trials / Sr
D) S = Transmission window / Time for message transmission
theory.explanation: The MARP Utilization slide defines it exactly this way: useful transmission time over the whole window (reservation phase + transmission phase). The two u/((u−v)+v/Sr)-style formulas are just this ratio worked out for the two cases (reservation frame carries data or not).

formulaApplication.question: In MARP, the data frame u = 500 bits, the reservation trial frame v = 5 bits (carrying no data of its own), and the reservation-phase utilization Sr = 0.5. What is the MARP utilization S?
In MARP, the data frame u = 2000 bits, the reservation frame v = 50 bits (and it DOES carry some of the data), and the reservation-phase utilization Sr = 0.6. What is the MARP utilization S?
A Wi-Fi network uses MARP at 5 Mbps. The data frame u = 800 bits, the reservation trial v = 20 bits carrying no data, and the reservation-phase MAC has utilization Sr = 0.4. What is the throughput?
In MARP, u = 1000 bits and v = 25 bits (reservation carries no data). What reservation-phase utilization Sr is needed to achieve an overall MARP utilization of 90%?
In MARP, the reservation-phase MAC protocol has utilization Sr = 0.2. What is the expected number of reservation trial frames needed per cycle?
formulaApplication.explanation: Number of trials X follows a geometric distribution: E[X] = 1/Sr = 1/0.2 = 5.

formulaApplication.question: In MARP, the data frame takes 5 ms and each reservation trial frame takes 0.5 ms. The reservation-phase utilization is Sr = 0.1. What is the average length of a full transmission window (reservation frame carries no data)?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Expected trials = 1/Sr = 10, so reservation phase takes 10 × 0.5 = 5 ms on average.
Window = u + v/Sr = 5 + 5 = 10 ms.

formulaApplication.question: MARP's reservation phase uses pure ALOHA running at pure ALOHA's own best possible utilization. The data frame u = 1000 bits and the reservation trial v = 15 bits, carrying no data. What is the MARP utilization S?
In MARP, u = 3000 bits and v = 100 bits, with the reservation frame carrying some of the data. The reservation-phase protocol has utilization Sr = 0.35. What is the MARP utilization S?

theory.question: In the MARP flowchart, what happens right after the "Transmit data frame" box?
options: A) The whole network shuts down
B) The station is permanently banned from transmitting again
C) Nothing — MARP only runs once ever
D) It jumps straight into a new data frame with no reservation phase
E) The cycle loops back to the Trial step, ready for the next transmission cycle
theory.explanation: The flowchart's arrow from "Transmit data frame" loops back up to the Trial diamond, showing that MARP repeats this reservation-then-transmission cycle continuously, one data frame at a time.

theory.question: The number of reservation trials X needed before one succeeds in MARP follows what kind of probability distribution?
theory.explanation: X = 1 with probability Sr, X = k with probability Sr(1−Sr)^(k−1) — that's the geometric distribution, which is exactly why E[X] = 1/Sr.

theory.question: The MARP Example slide teaches a problem-solving method called the CRACK Framework. What do the 5 letters stand for?
options: A) Check, Review, Apply, Calculate, Keep
B) Context, Rule, Answer, Compute, Know
C) Case, Reasoning, Answer, Check, Key
D) Context, fRamework, Apply, Calculation, checK
E) Collect, Review, Analyze, Compute, Keep
theory.explanation: CRACK: state the Context (what's given), identify the fRamework (which formula applies), Apply the numbers, do the Calculation, then checK the result makes sense (e.g. a utilization must satisfy S ≤ 1).

theory.question: When you calculate a MARP utilization S as a sanity check, what should always be true of the result?
options: A) S must equal Sr exactly
C) S must be an integer
theory.explanation: S is a utilization (useful time divided by total window time), so it can never exceed 1 (100%). If your calculated S comes out above 1, that's a sure sign of an arithmetic slip.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY24/25 Q1(10)]
Consider a packet switched network. Two nodes, node A and node D, are connected through two consecutive nodes B and C. A message of size 1000 bytes is transmitted from node A to node D (forwarded by B and then by C). The message is fragmented into five packets each with a 50-byte header. All links run the same data rate. If propagation delay is negligible, what is the minimum data rate for the links to achieve 140 ms of total transmission delay?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Each packet = 1000/5 + 50 = 250 bytes = 2000 bits. Hops = 3 (A–B, B–C, C–D).
Delay = (all packets on first hop) + (hops − 1) × 1 packet = (5 + 2) × 2000/R = 14,000/R
14,000/R ≤ 0.14 s, so R ≥ 100 kbps.

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY23/24 Q1(15)]
Station Rouse is sending a large message to Station Nouse. They are connected to each other by a packet switch router. The message is fragemented in two 1,000 bytes and one packet of 3000 bytes and transmitted using UDP. Determine the total transmission time, i.e. time from Station Rouse sending the first bit of the first packet to the last bit of the last packet been received by Station Nouse. The transmission rate is 1 Mbps and there is no other traffic on the network.
formulaApplication.explanation:
Tx times at 1 Mbps: 1000 B = 8 ms, 3000 B = 24 ms. Hops = 2.
First hop: all packets = 8 + 8 + 24 = 40 ms.
Then the last packet (3000 B) still needs the second hop: + 24 ms.
Total = 64 ms. (Unequal packets: the 'extra hops' term uses the LAST packet.)

formulaApplication.question:
[Past Finals AY25/26 Q1(15)]
Station Alpha is sending three packets to Station Beta through two packet switch routers. The packets sequence are of sizes 1000 bytes, 4000 bytes, and 2000 bytes. The transmission rate along the path is 2 Mbps. Calculate the total end-to-end transmission time from the moment Station Alpha begins transmitting the first bit of the first packet to when Station Beta receives the last bit of the last packet.
formulaApplication.explanation:
Tx times at 2 Mbps: 1000 B = 4 ms, 4000 B = 16 ms, 2000 B = 8 ms. 2 routers = 3 hops.
Trace it (each link sends one packet at a time):
Link 1: P1 0–4, P2 4–20, P3 20–28
Link 2: P1 4–8, P2 20–36, P3 36–44 (P3 waits for P2)
Link 3: P1 8–12, P2 36–52, P3 52–60
Total = 60 ms. The big middle packet blocks P3, so the simple 'last packet × extra hops' formula (28 + 2 × 8 = 44) doesn't work here.

formulaApplication.question: Each phone call is given 64 kb/s in a circuit-switched network. About how many simultaneous calls can a 10 Gb/s trunk carry?
A 5000-bit message is sent over a circuit-switched path with 4 hops at 50 kbps per link. Ignoring setup and propagation delays, what is the transmission delay?
formulaApplication.explanation:
Circuit switching: once the circuit is up, bits stream straight through.
Tx delay = data size / data rate = 5000 / 50k = 0.1 s = 100 ms, no matter how many hops.
400 ms wrongly adds a full transmission per hop (that's store-and-forward thinking).

formulaApplication.question: S sends 4 packets of 1000 bits each to D through the packet-switched path shown. Every link is 100 kbps. Ignoring propagation, processing and queuing delays, what is the total transmission delay?
formulaApplication.explanation:
1 packet takes 1000/100k = 10 ms per hop. Hops = 3.
Pipeline formula: all packets on the first hop + (hops − 1) × 1 packet
= 4 × 10 + 2 × 10 = 60 ms.
120 ms ignores the pipeline (4 packets × 3 hops).

formulaApplication.question: A 2400-byte message is split into 6 packets, each with a 40-byte header, and sent over 3 hops (2 intermediate nodes) at 1 Mbps. Ignoring propagation and processing delays, what is the total transmission delay?
formulaApplication.explanation:
